en: The Scripture on the Son Śyāma Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Śīlajin of the Qifu Qin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vairañjā with twelve hundred and fifty [monks].
Ten bhikṣus, along with an incalculable multitude of bodhisattvas, kings, ministers, elders, householders, laymen, and laywomen, all gathered together at one time.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“All of you, listen with minds tranquil and composed!

I recall my former lives, when I first attained the path of a bodhisattva. My ethical conduct was universal compassion; I practiced with diligence and single-mindedness, cultivating and accumulating wisdom and skillful means. The merit thus amassed is beyond measure or record, such that no devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, or common people were able to practice it.”
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to hear what you would say.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, countless eons ago, there was a bodhisattva named Sarvasucarita (All-Wondrous Conduct). Compassionate and benevolent, he bestowed gifts and rescued all living beings; he constantly practiced the four immeasurable minds, delivering the world from perils and nurturing those in suffering."

In the Tuṣita Heaven, he instructs the devas, constantly maintaining a concentrated mind during three periods of both day and night to contemplate the three realms, and illuminating and observing the paths of good and evil among the people throughout the ten directions.

Knowing those who recognize the existence of father and son, who provide for their parents, serve the Three Honored Ones, show reverence and obedience to their teachers and elders, and cultivate various meritorious virtues, he constantly surveys the five realms of existence with his divine eye.

"At that time, there was a country called Kāśī, where lived an elder who was solitary and without sons; both his eyes were blind. He wished in his heart to enter the mountains to seek unsurpassed wisdom, to cultivate pure resolve, and to take delight in the seclusion of empty and quiet places."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"This person has resolved to study the wondrous Way, yet both his eyes are blind; with no sight, he may fall into a mountain ravine or a ditch, or encounter venomous insects that would bring him harm.
If my life should end, I shall become his son and provide for my parents until the end of their lives."
He was immediately reborn into the home of blind parents as their son.
His parents loved him with great joy and affection; however, having set his mind on the Way and wishing to enter the mountains, he became attached to worldly fame because of the birth of this son.
When the son was ten years old, he was named Śyāma. He was supremely filial, compassionate, and benevolent, practicing the ten wholesome actions:

refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, deception, drinking alcohol, false speech, frivolous talk, and envy; he followed the Way without doubt and practiced with diligence day and night. He served his parents as one serves Heaven. His speech was always accompanied by a smile so as not to offend others' feelings; his conduct accorded with the Dharma and was free from any inclination toward depravity. Thereupon, his parents were filled with great joy and no longer had any sorrow.
When Śyāma was over ten years old, he knelt upright and addressed his parents, saying:
"I have originally resolved upon the Great Mind to enter the deep mountains, seeking the empty, quiescent, and unsurpassed Way. How could I abandon my fundamental vow for the sake of my son?"

Human beings dwelling in this world face the hundredfold changes of impermanence; life is not of stone or metal, and its end arrives without fixed date. I wish to fulfill my original intention and follow my former resolve: I shall enter the mountains together with my parents, providing for them with filial care at all appropriate times.
The parents replied to Śyāma, saying, "Your filial piety Heaven knows; do not violate your original vow, and you shall enter the mountains.
Śyāma immediately gave away all the possessions in his house to the poor throughout the kingdom, and then entered the mountains together with his parents.

When Śyāma reached the mountains, he used firewood and grass to build a house for his parents; he provided beds and mats so that they were neither cold nor hot, always remaining in a state of comfort.
Having entered the mountains for exactly one year, all the fruits have become abundant and exquisite; they are fragrant and sweet when eaten. Springs gush forth with water that is clear and cool.
Within the ponds, lotuses of five colors are brilliant and pure, while various sandalwood scents and the trees themselves are lush and flourishing, their fragrance twice as intense as usual.

The winds and rains came in their proper seasons, being neither too cold nor too hot. The leaves of the trees grew so close together as to shield them from the rain and dew, and the shade they provided kept the area beneath them perpetually cool.
Flying birds gathered there, all producing the sounds of music to entertain the blind parents.

Lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, wolves, and other venomous beasts all turned toward one another with hearts of compassion; they harbored no intent to alarm or harm, and as they drank water and ate fruit, they were entirely free from fear. Deer and various birds all came to dwell nearby, their voices harmonizing with those of Śyāma to entertain the blind parents.

Śyāma was the pinnacle of filial piety, benevolence, and compassion; he walked upon the earth ever fearing it might suffer pain. The celestial deities and mountain spirits all assumed human forms to console the three practitioners day and night, so that they could settle their minds in single-minded concentration, free from further sorrow.

"Śyāma constantly gathered a hundred kinds of fruits and melons with his parents to feed them. When his parents were thirsty and wished to drink, Śyāma would put on his deer-skin garment and carry a water jar to fetch water; even the wild deer and birds would come to drink from it without any fear or hesitation."
At that time, the King of Kāśī entered the mountains to hunt. Seeing deer and birds by the water’s edge, the king drew his bow and shot at them; by mistake, his arrow struck Śyāma.
Śyāma, struck by the poisoned arrow and in great pain, cried out loudly, "Who has taken a single poisoned arrow and shot and killed three practitioners of the Way?
Hearing the sound of a human voice, the king dismounted his horse and approached Śyāma; Śyāma then said to the king:

"The elephant dies because of its tusks; the rhinoceros dies because of its horn; the peacock dies because of its plumage; the deer dies because of its hide. Now I am dead without tusks, without horns, without hide or flesh, and am not fit to be eaten. What crime have I committed that I should be shot and killed so pointlessly?"
The king said, "Who are you?
You wear a deer-skin garment and are no different from birds and beasts."

Śyāma said, "I am a man from this kingdom who has come with my blind parents for more than twenty years to study the Way. Never before have I been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects; yet now I have been struck down and killed by the King's arrow."

"At that time, a great violent wind arose within the mountain, blowing and breaking the trees; birds, beasts, lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, wolves, and venomous creatures all let out cries that shook the entire mountain.
The sun lost its brilliant radiance, the flowing springs ran dry, the various flowers withered and died, and thunder and lightning shook the earth."
At that time, the blind parents suddenly rose in alarm and said, "What strange occurrence is this?
Śāṇa has been gone for a long time fetching water and has not yet returned; could it be that he has been harmed by venomous insects?"

"The birds and beasts cry out in grief; their calls and shrieks are unlike those of ordinary times. Winds arise from the four directions and the trees are broken and snapped; there must surely be some calamitous omen.
At that time, the king was struck with terror and deeply reproached himself:

"I originally went out to hunt deer, but by mistake my arrow wounded and killed this practitioner. His transgression is most grave; for the sake of craving a small amount of meat, I have incurred such heavy disaster. I shall now offer the wealth and treasures of the entire kingdom, my palace, my courtesans, the surrounding hills and moats, and all the cities and towns, in order to save my son's life."

Then the king stepped forward and attempted to pull the arrow from Śāṇa’s chest with his hand, but the shaft was so deep that it could not be extracted. Birds and beasts gathered from all directions like clouds; they wailed and cried out, making the entire mountain tremble.
The king became even more terrified, his limbs trembling all over.
Śyāma said, "This is not the fault of the King!

It is brought about by my own past karma. I do not begrudge my body or life; I only pity my blind parents, who are already advanced in years and have no sight. If I am gone suddenly, they too will surely perish. It is for this reason that I am so deeply distressed and tormented."
At that moment, all the devas, nāgas, and spirits were moved with solemn awe.
The King then spoke again:
"I would rather enter the hells and suffer punishment for a hundred kalpas than allow Śyāma’s life to be restored."
Kneeling long on his knees toward Śyāma, he repented his transgression:

"If your life should end, I shall no longer return to my kingdom, but will instead remain in these mountains to provide for your blind parents just as when you were here. Do not harbor any further thoughts of resentment; devas, nāgas, and spirits shall all bear witness that I do not violate this vow."

When Śyāma heard the king’s vow, he said, "Though I have been struck by a poisoned arrow, my heart is joyful and my mind is glad; though I die, I have no regrets. Entrust my parents to Your Majesty for their support; by doing so, Your Majesty shall be cleansed of guilt and attain immeasurable merit."
The King said, "Tell me where my parents are; I wish to know this before my son's life is cut short.
Śyāma then pointed them out:
"It is not far from this path; you will naturally see a thatched hut where my parents reside.
Your Majesty, proceed slowly so as not to startle or frighten my parents. Use skillful means to explain my intentions to them, and Your Majesty should report my case to my parents on my behalf."
"My impermanence has now arrived; I am about to depart for the next world.

It is not that I cherish my own body or life, but rather that I pity my blind parents, who are already advanced in years and have no sight. Should I suddenly be gone, they will have no one to rely upon or look up to, and it is for this reason that I am so distressed and torment myself."

My death is brought about by my own past transgressions; there is no way to escape it. Now I repent for all the evils I have committed since having taken on a body throughout incalculable kalpas. May these sins be extinguished here and now. I pray that I may meet with my parents in every lifetime, never to be separated from them, and that they may enjoy full longevity without any sorrow or affliction. May devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly follow, protect, and assist us, so that calamities are eliminated and all desires are fulfilled according to our wishes, spontaneously and without effort.
The king took several attendants and went to his parents' abode; after the king had departed, Śyāma suddenly died.
Hundreds of birds and beasts gathered from all sides like clouds, all wailing loudly as they circled Śyāma’s corpse, licking the blood from his chest.
Hearing these sounds, the blind parents became even more terrified and wandered about.
The king’s messenger moved quickly, brushing against the grasses and trees so that they rustled with a whistling sound;
the parents cried out in alarm, "Who is this person?"
"This is not the conduct of my son.
The king said, "I am the King of Kāśī.
Having heard that a blind man is practicing the Way in the mountains, I have come to make offerings to him."
The blind parents said:
"We have troubled Your Majesty to come and comfort us, traveling so far to this wilderness; we hope Your Majesty is not utterly exhausted and that your person remains at ease."
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, and the officials all well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, and are the five grains abundant?
Do the people of neighboring states not harm one another?
The king replied to the practitioner,
"I have been graced by your venerable kindness and have always remained in peace.
He then further inquired after his well-being:
"In this mountain, you have undergone great toil and hardship; amidst these trees, it must be very difficult to find rest. Are you at peace?

The blind parents replied, "By the grace of the Great King, we are always at peace. We have a filial son named Śyāma, who constantly gathers fruits and melons and fetches spring water so that we never lack anything."
"I have a grass mat; Your Majesty may sit upon it, and there are fruits and melons to eat.
Śyama has gone to fetch water and will return shortly.
When the king heard the words of the blind parents, his heart was again deeply pained, and he wept as he spoke these words:
"My transgression is indeed grave. Having entered the mountains to hunt, I saw a herd of deer by the water from afar; drawing my bow, I shot at them, but my arrow mistakenly struck Śāṇavāsa.
The ascetic’s son Śāṇavāsa has already been struck by the poisoned arrow, and his pain is most excruciating; that is why I have come here in person to speak to you, O ascetic."

Upon hearing this, the parents threw themselves to the ground, their bodies collapsing like the fall of Mount Tai and causing the earth to tremble violently. Wailing and looking up to heaven, they lamented, saying:
"Our son, Śyāma, was the most filial in all the world, beyond compare. He walked upon the earth ever fearing he might cause it pain; for what crime has he been shot and killed?"
"Just now, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing down and breaking the trees; the hundred birds cried out in sorrow, their loud wailing shaking the entire mountain.

I have lived in this mountain for over twenty years, yet never before have there been such calamitous portents. Now my son Śyāma has gone to fetch water and does not return; I fear there must be some cause for this, and thus all the deities are startled and move about in solemn agitation."
The mother then wept and wailed, refusing to stop; the father said, "Stop for now!
Among those born into this world, who is there that does not die?"
"When impermanence arrives, it cannot be warded off.
He then asked the king, "Where did you shoot Śyāma? Is he dead or alive now?"
The king related Śyāma’s words to his parents; hearing these words from the king, the blind parents were again overcome with profound grief:
"If we suddenly lose our son, we shall both surely die as well."
"Great King!
Please lead us two to our son's corpse.

The king immediately led the blind parents to the corpse; the father embraced his head and the mother embraced both his feet, placing him upon her lap. Each took both hands to feel for Śāṇa’s arrows, looking up to heaven and crying out:
"The various devas, nāgas, mountain deities, and tree deities all know that my son, Śyāma, was the most filial in the world."
"I am already old and my eyes can no longer see; it would be no regret for me to die in place of my son so that Śyāma may live.
Thereupon, the parents both made a solemn vow together:
"If Śyāma’s supreme filial piety is known to Heaven and Earth, then the arrow shall be drawn out, the poisonous pain shall be removed, and Śyāma shall be restored to life."

Thereupon, the throne of the second Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven trembled. Seeing with his own eyes these two blind practitioners of the Way embracing their son and wailing, he heard that from the fourth Tuṣita Heaven, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings came down from the celestial realm. In the time it takes a person to bend and stretch their arm, they arrived before Śyāma; they poured divine and wondrous medicine into Śyāma’s mouth. As the medicine entered his mouth, the arrow was extracted and the poison expelled, and he was restored to life as he was before.

When the parents heard that Śyāma had already been restored to life, both their eyes opened; birds and beasts all uttered sounds of great joy; the wind ceased and the clouds dispersed so that the sun shone with renewed brilliance; flowing springs gushed forth, pure and cool; the lotuses in the ponds were of five colors, radiant and exquisite; and the fragrance of various sandalwoods and trees was twice as fragrant as usual.

At that time, the king was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself; he prostrated before Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and then returned to pay homage to his parents and his son, Śyāma, saying:

"I wish to offer all the wealth and treasures of this entire kingdom to these practitioners of the Way so that we may provide for one another, thereby extinguishing my transgressions so that none remain."
Śyāma said to the king:
"If you wish to cultivate merit, Your Majesty should simply return to your kingdom and comfort your people, ensuring they uphold the precepts.
Do not engage in hunting or recklessly kill the innocent; otherwise, your person will find no peace, and at the end of your life, you shall enter the hells."

When people dwell in this world, affectionate attachments are but temporary; separation lasts long and one cannot remain forever together. Your Majesty, by virtue of past merit you have now become king; do not be arrogant in your sovereignty. Because of such self-indulgence, you may commit immeasurable evils and later fall into the evil realms—what benefit would there be in regretting it then?
The King replied, "As you have instructed.

The King's hunters saw that although Śyāma had died, he was restored to life by the medicine of a celestial deity; his parents' eyes were opened through such a miraculous transformation. They all received the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome deeds, so that upon death they attained rebirth in heaven and did not enter the evil realms.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"O all you who have gathered here!
He who was Śyāma in his past lives was my very self."
The blind father was King Śuddhodana;
the blind mother was the present King’s consort, Māyā;
and the King of the Kāśī country was Ānanda.
"The Śakra Devendra is Maitreya Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In my previous lives, as a son I was filial and kind; as a ruler I nurtured with compassion; as a subject I served with reverence. Thus, I have attained for myself the status of the Honored One of the Three Realms."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Śyāma’s Son.
